claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility because dislocations pile up at internal boundaries.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and premature failure during tensile loading.
A single-step, short-duration anneal at an intermediate temperature can modify the alloy microstructure.
The anneal can induce controlled segregation along lamellar boundaries.
The anneal can form coherent nanometric precipitates along lamellar boundaries.
Annealing temperature can influence the phase constitution and characteristic length scale of decomposition in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed coherent precipitates or segregated interfacial layers act as effective dislocation sinks.
The interfacial dislocation sinks reduce dislocation pile-ups and relax local stress concentrations.
Reducing pile-ups and stress concentrations mitigates microcracking and delays catastrophic damage during straining.
The annealed alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain the strength of the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy may have greater strength than the untreated alloy.
The beneficial response depends on optimization of annealing temperature and duration.
Excessive annealing can over-age and coarsen the precipitates, potentially reducing strength.
A controlled atmosphere during annealing will prevent oxidation and preserve the dual-phase microstructure.
The predicted benefit is applicable under room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing.
